content: The experience and availability of various types of healthcare providers and resources at the point of service delivery must be carefully considered when implementing medical guidelines. The Guideline Development Group (GDG), convened by the World Health Organization (WHO) on multiple occasions in 2013 and 2014, comprised 68 individuals representing a broad spectrum of stakeholders. Their primary task was to review and, where necessary, revise the guidance in the fourth edition of the Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (MEC) to develop the fifth edition. During this revision process, the GDG prioritized the review of six topics deemed critical to the field or those with new evidence that could necessitate changes to existing recommendations. Additionally, they reviewed two topics for which interim guidance had been issued after the publication of the fourth edition, contraceptive eligibility recommendations for four new contraceptive methods, and two topics requiring greater clarity in recommendations from the fourth edition, as requested by the Guidelines Review Committee. In total, recommendations for 14 topics were reviewed for the fifth edition of the MEC. To formulate recommendations using the four MEC categories for contraceptive eligibility, the GDG considered potential harms associated with contraceptive use, GRADE evidence profiles, the benefits of preventing unintended pregnancies, and an approach that prioritized the availability of a wide range of contraceptive options. Decisions were reached through consensus, involving discussion, debate, and expert consultation to resolve disagreements. For certain recommendations, clarification statements were added to provide further explanation or guidance on interpreting the numerical classification. For each contraceptive method, the GDG evaluated the potential benefits and risks of its use concerning specific medical conditions or medically relevant physiological or personal characteristics, such as age, breastfeeding status, or smoking habits. In many cases, no new evidence was identified since the publication of the fourth edition of the MEC in 2009, or emerging evidence confirmed previous research findings. Consequently, many recommendations from the fourth edition were reviewed and reaffirmed without changes. For these unchanged recommendations, the WHO Secretariat updated the evidence statements, references, and citations in the contraceptive method tables in Part II of the document. WHO plans to initiate a review of the recommendations in this document in four years. In the interim, WHO will continue to monitor the body of evidence informing these recommendations and convene additional consultations as needed if new evidence necessitates reconsideration of existing recommendations. Updates may be particularly warranted for issues where the evidence base evolves rapidly. Interim recommendations will be made available on WHO’s sexual and reproductive health web pages. WHO also encourages research to address unresolved issues related to establishing medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use and invites comments and suggestions for improving this guidance. The GDG reviewed 14 topics, encompassing over 575 recommendations, during the 2014 revision of the MEC. The GRADE approach was applied to assess the quality of available evidence, forming the basis for the recommendations. For some topics, multiple outcomes of interest and/or contraceptive methods were examined, with GRADE assessments presented as either a single assessment or a range reflecting the quality of evidence across important outcomes or contraceptive methods. For combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs), the following recommendations were made: Women aged 40 years and older can generally use CHCs (MEC Category 2). Breastfeeding women less than six weeks postpartum should not use CHCs (MEC Category 4). Breastfeeding women between six weeks and six months postpartum should generally not use CHCs (MEC Category 3). Breastfeeding women six months postpartum or later can generally use CHCs (MEC Category 2). Postpartum women less than 21 days without other risk factors for venous thromboembolism (VTE) should generally not use CHCs (MEC Category 3). Those with other VTE risk factors should not use CHCs (MEC Category 4). Women 21 to 42 days postpartum without other VTE risk factors can generally use CHCs (MEC Category 2), while those with other VTE risk factors should generally not use CHCs (MEC Category 3). Women more than 42 days postpartum can use CHCs without restriction (MEC Category 1). For women with superficial venous disorders: Women with varicose veins can use CHCs without restriction (MEC Category 1). Women with superficial venous thrombosis (SVT) can generally use CHCs (MEC Category 2). For progestogen-only contraceptives (POCs) and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine devices (LNG-IUDs) among breastfeeding women: Breastfeeding women less than six weeks postpartum can generally use progestogen-only pills (POPs) and implants (MEC Category 2) but should generally not use progestogen-only injectables (POIs) (MEC Category 3). Breastfeeding women six weeks to six months postpartum can use POPs, POIs, and implants without restriction (MEC Category 1). Breastfeeding women six months postpartum or later can use POPs, POIs, and implants without restriction (MEC Category 1). Breastfeeding women less than 48 hours postpartum can generally use LNG-IUDs (MEC Category 2). However, those 48 hours to four weeks postpartum should generally not have an LNG-IUD inserted (MEC Category 3). Women four weeks postpartum or later can use LNG-IUDs without restriction (MEC Category 1). Women with puerperal sepsis should not have an LNG-IUD inserted (MEC Category 4). For emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs): ECPs are not applicable for pregnant women. Breastfeeding women can use combined oral contraceptives (COCs) or levonorgestrel (LNG) for ECPs without restriction (MEC Category 1). They can generally use ulipristal acetate (UPA) for ECPs (MEC Category 2). Women with a history of ectopic pregnancies, severe cardiovascular disease, migraines, or severe liver disease can generally use COCs, LNG, or UPA for ECPs (MEC Category 2). There are no restrictions on repeated use of ECPs or their use in cases of rape (MEC Category 1). For intrauterine devices (IUDs) in women at increased risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs): Many women at increased STI risk can generally initiate copper-bearing IUDs (Cu-IUDs) or LNG-IUDs (MEC Category 2). Women at increased STI risk can generally continue using Cu-IUDs or LNG-IUDs (MEC Category 2). For women at high risk of HIV infection, living with HIV, or using antiretroviral therapy (ART): Women at high risk of HIV can use all hormonal contraceptive methods without restriction (MEC Category 1). They can generally use LNG-IUDs (MEC Category 2). Women living with asymptomatic or mild HIV clinical disease (WHO Stage 1 or 2) can use all hormonal contraceptive methods without restriction (MEC Category 1) and can generally use LNG-IUDs (MEC Category 2). Women living with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO Stage 3 or 4) should generally not initiate LNG-IUD use (MEC Category 3) until their condition improves to asymptomatic or mild disease. However, those already using LNG-IUDs need not have them removed (MEC Category 2 for continuation). Women using nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) can use all hormonal contraceptive methods without restriction (MEC Category 1). They can generally use LNG-IUDs (MEC Category 2) if their HIV clinical disease is asymptomatic or mild. Women with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease should generally not initiate LNG-IUD use (MEC Category 3) until their condition improves. Those already using LNG-IUDs need not have them removed (MEC Category 2 for continuation).
